Finding: Contract type is the single strongest churn driver, both statistically and predictively.
Evidence: Month-to-month customers churn at 42.71% vs. 2.83% for Two-year customers (15.1x higher). Contract ranks #1 in the combined statistical + model-based driver table (Cramer's V effect size: Medium; top Random Forest & permutation importance).
Why It Matters: Contract commitment length is both the clearest lever the business controls and the highest-leverage predictor available — it outranks pricing, tenure, and every service variable.
Possible Business Reason: Month-to-month customers face zero switching penalty and are re-solicited constantly by competitors; long contracts create structural exit friction and typically bundle in a discount that raises the psychological cost of leaving.
Recommended Action: Launch an active contract-migration program: incentivize month-to-month customers (especially high-risk segments) to move to 1- or 2-year terms via modest discounts, device-free upgrades, or loyalty pricing locks.
Expected Business Impact: Month-to-month customers are 3875 of the base and contribute 88.55% of all churn — even a modest migration rate could materially cut total churn.
Confidence / Limitation: Correlational: contract type is chosen by the customer (self-selection), so migrating a customer to a longer contract may not reduce their churn propensity by the same margin observed cross-sectionally — some of the effect may reflect that already-loyal customers self-select into longer contracts.

Finding: Nearly half of all churn happens in a customer's first 6 months.
Evidence: The 0-6 month tenure band holds only 21.03% of the customer base but accounts for 41.95% of all churn, at a 52.94% churn rate — nearly 8x the 6.61% rate seen in customers with 61+ months tenure.
Why It Matters: This is an onboarding problem, not a loyalty problem — most churn is concentrated in a narrow, addressable window right after acquisition.
Possible Business Reason: New customers are disproportionately on month-to-month contracts (95.4% of this band) and have adopted very few services yet (avg 2.72 vs. 5.83 for 61+ month customers) — they haven't yet formed the habits or bundle commitments that create stickiness.
Recommended Action: Build a structured 90-day onboarding journey: proactive check-ins at day 30/60/90, an early-tenure discount or waived setup fee tied to add-on adoption (e.g., free trial of Online Security/Tech Support), and a dedicated new-customer support queue.
Expected Business Impact: Reducing first-6-month churn by even 10 percentage points (from 52.94% toward ~43%) would retain roughly 148 additional customers per cohort of this size.
Confidence / Limitation: High confidence on the pattern (large sample, consistent across contract/service cuts); the exact causal lever (price vs. service vs. support) is not isolated by this cross-sectional data alone.

Finding: Electronic check payers churn at nearly 3x the rate of customers on automatic payment methods.
Evidence: Electronic check churn rate is 45.29% vs. 15.24% for the lowest-risk automatic method — a gap of 30.0 percentage points. PaymentMethod is also statistically significant (Chi-square, Medium effect) and ranks in the top 10 combined churn drivers.
Why It Matters: Payment method is a low-cost, low-friction lever the business can act on directly through product design (defaults, incentives) rather than pricing.
Possible Business Reason: Manual electronic-check payment is more failure-prone (declined payments, forgotten manual renewals) and self-selects for customers who have not committed to an ongoing automated relationship with the provider — it may also proxy for lower price sensitivity to switching.
Recommended Action: Incentivize migration to autopay (bank transfer or credit card) with a small permanent monthly credit or one-time bill credit; make autopay the default option at signup and during the checkout/renewal flow.
Expected Business Impact: Electronic check represents 2365 customers (33.6% of the base); shifting even a quarter of them to autopay, if the churn gap holds, could prevent a meaningful share of overall churn.
Confidence / Limitation: Correlational — payment method may partly proxy for other unobserved risk factors (e.g., financial engagement level) rather than being a pure causal driver.

Finding: The combination of Month-to-month + Fiber optic + Electronic check is the single highest-risk customer profile identified.
Evidence: This combination churns at 60.37%, covering 1307 customers (18.56% of the base) at an average MonthlyCharges of $87.18.
Why It Matters: This is a compounding-risk profile: three independently significant risk factors stack, producing churn far above any single factor alone — this is exactly the kind of customer a proactive retention program should flag first.
Possible Business Reason: These customers pay premium fiber pricing without the security of a contract discount, and without the convenience/stickiness of automatic billing — the profile combines maximum price sensitivity with minimum switching friction.
Recommended Action: Build a real-time 'triple-risk' flag in the CRM for customers matching this exact combination and route them into a white-glove retention track (proactive call, personalized discount, or bundled contract-plus-autopay offer) before they show churn signals.
Expected Business Impact: This segment alone represents ~$68,788 in monthly revenue currently walking out the door at the observed churn rate.
Confidence / Limitation: High confidence — large sample size (>1,300 customers) and consistent with each individual factor's independently confirmed effect.

Finding: Customers without Online Security or Tech Support churn at roughly 2.7x the rate of customers who have them — but this is confounded with Internet Service type.
Evidence: Non-users of Online Security churn at 41.77% vs. 14.61% for users (a 27.16 point gap); Tech Support shows a nearly identical pattern (41.64% vs. 15.17%).
Why It Matters: These are the two highest-impact add-on services for retention — larger effect than Streaming TV/Movies, which show only a ~3-4 point gap.
Possible Business Reason: Online Security and Tech Support are 'peace of mind' / support-oriented services; customers who skip them may be more price-sensitive or have had less positive early support experiences, and also lack a proactive touchpoint with the company that could catch dissatisfaction early.
Recommended Action: Bundle Online Security + Tech Support as a free trial (first 2-3 months) for new sign-ups, especially in the high-risk Month-to-month + Fiber optic segment; make these two add-ons a proactive up-sell target rather than passive product-catalog items.
Expected Business Impact: 3498 customers currently lack Online Security — even a modest uptake among high-risk segments could shift meaningful churn volume given the 27-point rate gap.
Confidence / Limitation: Confounded with Internet Service type (fiber-optic customers show both lower add-on attach rates and higher baseline churn) — the effect is likely partly, not wholly, attributable to the add-ons themselves; a controlled offer test is needed to isolate the causal lift.

Finding: Fiber optic customers churn at nearly double the rate of DSL customers despite (or because of) paying premium prices.
Evidence: Fiber optic churn rate: 41.89% vs. DSL — a gap confirmed as statistically significant (Chi-square, Medium effect; ranks #5 in the combined driver table). Fiber customers also carry the highest average MonthlyCharges of any internet segment.
Why It Matters: This suggests a value-perception or service-quality problem specific to the fiber product line, not just a generic 'higher price = more churn' relationship (DSL and no-internet customers pay far less and churn far less).
Possible Business Reason: Possible explanations include competitive fiber offers from rivals, reliability/installation complaints specific to fiber, or a price/perceived-value mismatch where fiber's premium isn't matched by proportionally higher perceived service quality or bundled support.
Recommended Action: Commission a targeted fiber-customer satisfaction/exit-survey study to isolate whether the driver is price, reliability, or competitive offers; pilot a fiber-specific loyalty price lock or service-quality guarantee.
Expected Business Impact: The 'Fiber-Optic High-Risk' segment defined later in this report holds 40.6% of total MRR on its own — even a small improvement here has an outsized revenue impact.
Confidence / Limitation: Root cause is not identifiable from this dataset alone (no service-quality, NPS, or competitor-offer fields present) — this is flagged as a priority for further data collection, not a settled conclusion.

Finding: Service bundle depth has a non-linear, hump-shaped relationship with churn — the riskiest customers are not the ones with the fewest services.
Evidence: Churn rate rises from 10.92% at 1 service to a peak of 44.92% at 3 services, then falls steadily to 5.29% at the full 9-service bundle.
Why It Matters: A simple 'more services = more sticky' assumption would miss this risk group entirely — mid-bundle customers (often fiber internet + a couple of add-ons, still on month-to-month) are actually the highest-risk group, not the lowest.
Possible Business Reason: Customers with only 1 service are often DSL-only or phone-only (low price, low-risk-profile by nature); customers with 3-4 services have made a moderate commitment (often to premium fiber) without yet reaching full-bundle lock-in, making them price-sensitive but not yet retained by switching costs.
Recommended Action: Target upsell campaigns at the 2-4 service range specifically — push these customers toward fuller bundles (5+) rather than assuming any add-on sale reduces risk equally.
Expected Business Impact: The 3-service group alone has a 44.92% churn rate across 846 customers — a clearly identifiable, sizeable target list for a bundle-completion campaign.
Confidence / Limitation: Correlational and likely confounded by contract type and internet type, which independently correlate with both bundle size and churn.

Finding: Revenue at risk from churn is substantial: an estimated $1,669,570 in annualized revenue is tied to customers who have already churned.
Evidence: Churned customers represented $139,130.85 in monthly recurring revenue (30.5% of total MRR) at the time they left — churned customers actually had HIGHER average MonthlyCharges ($74.44) than retained customers ($61.27).
Why It Matters: The business is not just losing customer count — it is disproportionately losing its higher-paying customers on a per-month basis, even though (due to short tenure) their lifetime TotalCharges were lower.
Possible Business Reason: Higher MonthlyCharges customers are concentrated in fiber/high-bundle segments that, as shown above, carry structurally higher churn risk — the business's premium product line is also its leakiest.
Recommended Action: Treat revenue-at-risk (not just churn count) as the primary retention KPI; prioritize save-desk resources by MonthlyCharges x churn-probability rather than by raw churn-probability alone.
Expected Business Impact: Even a 5-percentage-point reduction in overall churn rate would protect roughly $273,663 in annualized revenue.
Confidence / Limitation: The annualized figure is a simple run-rate extrapolation (last observed MonthlyCharges x 12) and does not account for win-back, natural re-acquisition, or discounting during any retention offer.

Finding: Senior citizens are a small (16.2% of base) but disproportionately high-risk segment.
Evidence: Senior citizens churn at 41.68% vs. the 26.5% company average, and SeniorCitizen is a statistically significant churn factor.
Why It Matters: A demographic segment this identifiable is an easy, low-cost targeting criterion for a dedicated retention track, distinct from behavioral/contract-based segments.
Possible Business Reason: Senior customers may be more sensitive to billing complexity, less likely to be on autopay/paperless billing, or more responsive to a personal-service retention approach than a self-service digital one.
Recommended Action: Pilot a senior-focused support line or simplified billing/contract option, and test whether a human-assisted (vs. digital-only) retention outreach improves save rates for this group specifically.
Expected Business Impact: Because this is a demographic (not behavioral) segment, it is straightforward to identify at signup and route into a differentiated onboarding/support track from day one.
Confidence / Limitation: SeniorCitizen effect size is 'Small' in the combined statistical test — real but modest; should be one input among several in a targeting model, not a stand-alone trigger.

Finding: Customers without Partners or Dependents churn more — household stability correlates with retention.
Evidence: Both Partner and Dependents are statistically significant churn factors (Chi-square, Small effect each); customers with neither show meaningfully higher churn than customers with both.
Why It Matters: This is a low-cost, already-collected signal that can improve risk scoring without any new data collection.
Possible Business Reason: Customers with partners/dependents likely have more stable household circumstances, more shared decision-making friction around switching providers, and potentially bundle household services more fully.
Recommended Action: Include household-composition fields in the churn-risk score used for outreach prioritization; no new product action is implied on their own, but they sharpen targeting.
Expected Business Impact: Marginal — these are reinforcing signals for the risk model rather than an independent actionable lever.
Confidence / Limitation: Small effect size — should not be over-weighted in isolation; useful mainly as a model feature.

Finding: The customer base is structurally skewed toward the highest-risk contract type, amplifying total churn exposure.
Evidence: 3875 of 7043.0 customers (55.0%) are on month-to-month contracts — more than double the combined one-year and two-year population.
Why It Matters: Even without any change in per-segment churn rates, the sheer size of the month-to-month population means the company's blended churn rate will remain structurally elevated unless contract mix shifts.
Possible Business Reason: Flexible plans are likely a deliberate acquisition strategy (lower barrier to sign up), but the acquisition-friendly design directly conflicts with the retention goal.
Recommended Action: Reframe contract-term selection at the point of sale — present 1-year terms as the default with a visible discount, rather than month-to-month as the unmarked default option.
Expected Business Impact: Shifting even 10% of the month-to-month base to annual contracts would be expected (based on the 2.83% vs 42.71% gap) to meaningfully lower blended churn over time.
Confidence / Limitation: This is a mix-shift recommendation with a plausible but untested magnitude — actual impact depends on whether migrated customers behave like organic long-contract customers or retain some of their original risk profile.

Finding: High-value, loyal customers are being retained well today — the risk is concentrated elsewhere, not here.
Evidence: The 'High-Value Loyal Customers' segment (1946) and 'Loyal Long-Term Customers' segment show churn rates of 14.48% and 6.68% respectively — both well below the 26.5% company average.
Why It Matters: This confirms the retention problem is concentrated and addressable (new/month-to-month/fiber customers) rather than diffuse across the whole base — a targeted strategy is appropriate, not a blanket price cut or broad win-back campaign.
Possible Business Reason: Long-tenured, high-value customers have already survived the highest-risk early window and are likely on favorable, stable contract/pricing arrangements.
Recommended Action: Protect (don't over-invest in) this segment with light-touch loyalty perks; concentrate new retention budget on the high-risk segments identified above.
Expected Business Impact: Avoids wasted retention spend on a segment that is not actually at risk, freeing budget for the higher-impact segments.
Confidence / Limitation: High confidence given large sample size and consistency across two independently defined loyal segments.

Finding: A predictive model can identify likely churners well above chance, enabling proactive (not just reactive) retention — but model choice should follow business usefulness (recall), not ROC-AUC alone.
Evidence: Gradient Boosting has the highest ROC-AUC (0.8468) but only 47.8% recall on the churn class, meaning it misses more than half of actual churners. Random Forest, at a nearly identical ROC-AUC (0.8449), catches 77.3% of actual churners — the better choice for a retention use case where missing a churner is costlier than one extra outreach call.
Why It Matters: Picking a model on ROC-AUC alone would deploy a system that silently misses most of the customers it was built to catch — recall on the churn class is the metric that actually maps to business value here (each miss is a lost customer with no chance at a save offer).
Possible Business Reason: Gradient Boosting optimizes for overall separability without accounting for the asymmetric cost of a false negative (a missed churner) vs. a false positive (one avoidable retention call) in this business context.
Recommended Action: Deploy Random Forest (or Logistic Regression, which shows a similar recall/AUC trade-off) as the production scoring model; score the active base monthly and route the top-risk decile to the retention team before they show explicit cancellation intent.
Expected Business Impact: At 77% recall, a monthly scoring process would surface the large majority of customers who go on to churn, giving the retention team a genuine head start versus a reactive, cancellation-triggered process.
Confidence / Limitation: Model trained and evaluated on historical, cross-sectional data; performance on live, future data should be monitored and the model periodically retrained. Precision of 54% means a substantial share of flagged customers will not actually churn — outreach cost per contact should stay low enough to make that acceptable.

Finding: Paperless billing customers churn at roughly double the rate of paper-bill customers.
Evidence: PaperlessBilling=Yes churns at 33.57% vs. 16.33% for paper-bill customers — statistically significant with a Small effect size.
Why It Matters: Counter-intuitively, a 'more digital / more modern' billing preference correlates with higher, not lower, churn — likely because paperless billing correlates heavily with month-to-month, digitally-native, price-comparison-savvy customers rather than being a driver in its own right.
Possible Business Reason: Customers who opt into paperless billing tend to be more digitally engaged and more likely to be comparison-shopping online, and paperless billing is also disproportionately common among month-to-month subscribers in this dataset.
Recommended Action: Do not treat paperless billing itself as a lever to change; instead use it only as a scoring signal, and ensure billing communications for this group include clear renewal/retention messaging (since they are less likely to see a physical mail touchpoint).
Expected Business Impact: Improves risk-model precision at near-zero cost since the field is already collected.
Confidence / Limitation: Very likely confounded with contract type and digital engagement; not recommended as a standalone causal target for intervention.

Finding: Gender and basic phone service show no meaningful relationship with churn.
Evidence: Both gender (p=0.49) and PhoneService (p=0.34) are not statistically significant at alpha=0.05, and both rank at the bottom of the combined importance table.
Why It Matters: These fields can be safely excluded from targeted retention messaging and campaign personalization — there is no evidence they differentiate risk.
Possible Business Reason: Phone service is now a commodity/legacy product for this business (90%+ penetration) with little differentiation power; gender is not expected to relate to a B2C telecom churn decision.
Recommended Action: Deprioritize any planned gender- or phone-service-based segmentation for retention purposes; focus resources on the confirmed high-signal variables instead.
Expected Business Impact: Avoids wasted analytical and campaign design effort on non-predictive dimensions.
Confidence / Limitation: Absence of evidence in this dataset; do not generalize to claim these factors are irrelevant in all contexts or geographies.

Finding: TotalCharges is negatively associated with churn even though MonthlyCharges is positively associated — the two 'charges' variables point in opposite directions.
Evidence: Point-biserial correlation with Churn: TotalCharges r = -0.198 (negative, Small effect) vs. MonthlyCharges r = 0.193 (positive, Small effect).
Why It Matters: This is not a contradiction — it reflects that TotalCharges is dominated by tenure (customers who stayed longer accumulated more total billing), while MonthlyCharges reflects current price level. Reading 'charges' as a single concept would produce the wrong conclusion.
Possible Business Reason: Long-tenured (low-churn) customers have naturally high TotalCharges simply by virtue of having paid for many months, regardless of their monthly rate.
Recommended Action: Never use TotalCharges alone as a 'high value = safe' signal without controlling for tenure; use AverageChargePerMonth or MonthlyCharges together with tenure for value-risk scoring instead.
Expected Business Impact: Prevents a costly targeting mistake (e.g., wrongly deprioritizing a genuinely at-risk long-tenure, high-MonthlyCharges customer because their TotalCharges looks reassuring).
Confidence / Limitation: Statistical relationship is clear; the practical modeling implication (feature engineering nuance) is an interpretive recommendation, not a directly tested claim.

Finding: The safest identifiable customer profile — Two-year contract + automatic payment — churns at under 3%, a useful retention 'north star' profile.
Evidence: Two year + Automatic payment (bank/credit) churns at only 2.79% across 1145 customers.
Why It Matters: This profile defines the practical floor of achievable churn for this business given current products — it's a concrete, evidence-based target state for migration campaigns rather than an abstract goal.
Possible Business Reason: Long contract term removes the easy-exit option and automatic payment removes the passive/friction churn pathway — the two levers the business most directly controls are both engaged simultaneously in this group.
Recommended Action: Use this exact combination as the explicit 'target state' messaging in contract-migration and autopay-adoption campaigns ('customers like you churn at under 3%').
Expected Business Impact: Provides a concrete, defensible ROI baseline when modeling the expected impact of migration campaigns.
Confidence / Limitation: Small residual churn (2.79%) likely reflects unavoidable reasons (relocation, death, business closure) rather than addressable dissatisfaction — treat as a practical floor, not zero.

Finding: Multiple Lines and Streaming services show only weak, borderline associations with churn.
Evidence: MultipleLines shows a Negligible effect size despite a statistically significant p-value (a common pattern with this sample size, where even small differences become 'significant'); StreamingTV/StreamingMovies show only a Small effect and a ~3-4 point user-vs-non-user churn gap — much smaller than Online Security or Tech Support.
Why It Matters: Not every statistically significant result is business-significant; prioritization should follow effect size, not p-value alone.
Possible Business Reason: Streaming and multiple-line services are largely entertainment/convenience add-ons with weaker ties to the core support-and-reliability concerns that appear to drive most churn.
Recommended Action: Do not prioritize streaming-service upsell campaigns as a retention tool; reserve that budget for Online Security/Tech Support bundling, which shows a much larger effect.
Expected Business Impact: Redirects limited retention-offer budget toward higher-yield levers.
Confidence / Limitation: Large sample size means even small, low-business-relevance effects register as 'statistically significant' — effect size (not the p-value) should drive prioritization decisions.

Finding: The High-Value Churn Risk segment is small but carries an outsized dollar cost per lost customer.
Evidence: This segment (395 customers, 5.61% of the base) churns at 32.66% with an average MonthlyCharges of $95.88 — losing one of these customers costs roughly 1.5x the revenue of losing an average customer.
Why It Matters: Retention ROI is highest here: the cost of a proactive discount or outreach is small relative to the revenue at stake per customer, unlike in low-value segments where the same offer may not be cost-justified.
Possible Business Reason: These are customers who have both accumulated meaningful lifetime value AND remain on a high-risk (month-to-month) contract structure — likely price-conscious premium users who haven't yet been 'locked in.'
Recommended Action: Create a dedicated white-glove retention track for this segment with a named account owner / concierge support line and a contract-migration offer with a richer discount than the mass-market offer.
Expected Business Impact: This segment alone represents $12,649.25 in monthly revenue already lost to churn — protecting even a fraction of the remainder has a large per-customer payback.
Confidence / Limitation: Small absolute segment size (n=395) means statistical estimates are noisier than for larger segments — validate the retention-offer ROI with a pilot before scaling budget.
